author: Claude (English teacher role), v2 against the v2 quality gate
basis: Full rewrite. The previous overlay kept most of the workbook B1 column, which carried a B2 lexical load (long-word share above 20% on seven slides, Flesch-Kincaid 13.1 on slide 6) and repeated the A2 wording on slides 1, 4 and 8. This version is built on B1 grammar rather than B1 synonyms: present perfect (slides 2 and 12), a first conditional (slide 7), relative clauses (slides 3, 4, 7, 9, 12), a because-clause (slide 6) and time clauses (slides 3 and 11), with everyday mid-length words so the long-word share stays inside the B1 band. Meaning, slide order and every named fact are unchanged: SDG 9 Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure; ChatGPT; Gemini; AI hallucination; Google Scholar; PubMed. Technical corrections: the workbook B1 says the model 'runs on math formulas that predict the next word from patterns found across the internet' and that 'the data and the papers behind them are sometimes invented by the computer'. Restated as training on a large body of human writing and selection of the most likely next word, and as fabricated sources rather than fabricated data. No claim that the model knows, understands or looks anything up.

slides.1: Good morning. My topic is SDG 9, the goal for Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure. The United Nations wants every state to invest in better factories and in the new tools that follow them.
slides.2: Inside that goal, AI has become a new kind of digital infrastructure. It lets researchers handle enormous data sets and reach results sooner, but can we rely on it?
slides.3: As science majors, most of us open ChatGPT or Gemini before we open a textbook. These systems tidy our lab reports and shorten long articles. They explain difficult theory that would otherwise cost us hours.
slides.4: However, the output is not always correct. These tools sometimes produce papers, authors and results that were never real, and scientists call that strange failure an AI hallucination.
slides.5: To see why, remember what a language model actually does. It was trained on an enormous library of human writing. It selects each word simply by how likely that word is to follow.
slides.6: A smooth paragraph can be pure invention, because the system continues a sentence instead of testing a claim. Probability is not proof, and nothing inside the tool will warn you.
slides.7: If we paste invented sources into an assignment, we will lose marks at once. Worse, we damage our honesty and the trust that every future scientist has to earn.
slides.8: The harm does not stop at the classroom door. When false claims reach the public, confidence in research falls, and a society that distrusts science will never accept the innovations it needs.
slides.9: So how should we work with these systems? Critical thinking has to come first, which means treating every answer as a temporary draft that we still have to verify.
slides.10: Next, confirm each source in an academic database such as Google Scholar or PubMed. The tool can gather material far quicker than we can, yet the final decision belongs to us.
slides.11: Even in a modern laboratory, the human element is still essential. A machine can organise enormous amounts of data. But it feels no curiosity, no doubt and no shame when a claim is false.
slides.12: AI may be the most exciting invention that SDG 9 has delivered. Yet a tool without a responsible user simply spreads false information faster. Use it, verify it, and science keeps the trust it has earned.
